CausalChain: Nutritive intervention (e.g., branched‐chain amino acids) -> Enhanced hepatocyte albumin synthesis -> Increased serum albumin levels -> Lower (more favorable) ALBI score -> Improved liver functional reserve -> Increased treatment tolerance and improved efficacy of systemic HCC therapies
Hypothesis: Targeted nutritional or hepatoprotective interventions that boost albumin synthesis in HCC patients can improve the ALBI grade, thereby enhancing tolerance to and efficacy of systemic therapies, ultimately leading to better clinical outcomes.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), liver function preserved by adequate albumin synthesis is critical for both prognosis and treatment tolerance. The albumin‐bilirubin (ALBI) grade, which relies exclusively on objective measures of liver synthetic function, not only stratifies patients’ outcomes across multiple treatment modalities but also reflects the dynamic interplay between hepatocyte function and systemic therapies. We propose that interventions designed to augment or preserve hepatocyte albumin production, such as nutritional supplementation with branched‐chain amino acids or other hepatoprotective modalities, may improve the ALBI grade, thereby enhancing eligibility for and response to systemic therapies including targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors. This hypothesis has the potential to drive novel interventional studies aimed at liver functional rehabilitation to optimize therapeutic outcomes in HCC.
